sentences.text: Rhamphosuchus was an extinct genus of gavialoid crocodilians that lived in the Indian subcontinent. These animals were large-bodied crocodilians characterized by elongated and narrow jaws typical of the gavialoid group.
Unlike modern gharials, Rhamphosuchus species were more robust, possessing snouts that widened toward the head and closely spaced teeth forming an alligator-like overbite.
The tip of the lower jaw was less expanded than in derived gavialoids and remained closer in width to the rest of the mandibular symphysis.
Each premaxilla contained five teeth, a count matching modern Indian gharials but exceeding that of adult false gharials by one.
Deep pits pierced by small foramina on the upper jaw may have functioned as insertion points for a sensory structure.
Rhamphosuchus crassidens could reach body lengths of 8 to 11 meters based on rigorous estimates of known specimens.
However, a more recent study suggests the animal measured 8 to 11 meters in length, and therefore is not the largest known crocodilian.
Fossils of chalicotheres and rhinos found in the same formations bear bitemarks from a large crocodilian.
The genus Rhamphosuchus was described by Richard Lydekker in 1886.
The holotype, defined as the specimen the species is based on, is a partial snout tip catalogued as NHMUK PV OR 39802.
Gudrun Corvinus and H. Hermann Schleich described a snout tip from Rato Khola and isolated teeth from Surai Khola as part of the Surai Khola Formation.
Early researcher Richard Lydekker estimated Rhamphosuchus crassidens reached a length of 15 to 18 meters.

Researchers suggest Rhamphosuchus had a generalist diet due to its robust build and large size, unlike the mostly fish-eating gharial. It is possible that Rhamphosuchus attacked other crocodilians, supported by bite marks found on Miocene Gavialis fossils.
Rhamphosuchus may have preyed on chalicotheres, rhinos, and possibly juvenile Paraceratherium.
Analysis of Rhamphosuchus pachyrhynchus shows its snout width increased much more rapidly than other skull dimensions during growth.
Courville and colleagues note that Rhamphosuchus pachyrhynchus had teeth that became much more tightly packed together than in modern gavialoids as it aged.
Warm temperatures, extensive wetlands, and high ecosystem productivity likely allowed Rhamphosuchus to grow to its large size.
Walter and colleagues hypothesize that gigantism in crocodyliforms like Rhamphosuchus was driven by extensive marine or wetland biomes.
Rhamphosuchus probably had a more generalized carnivorous diet than the ichthyophagy of other tomistomine crocodilians.
Scientists debate whether Rhamphosuchus is a relative of the modern false gharial (Tomistominae) or the Indian gharial (Gavialoidea).
The precise phylogenetic position of Rhamphosuchus within Gavialoidea remains uncertain among researchers.
Gavialis leptodus was speculated to represent a juvenile Rhamphosuchus.
Rhamphosuchus crassidens lacks the expanded snout tip found in R. pachyrhynchus.
Fossils of Rhamphosuchus date to the Possibly Early Middle Pleistocene.
The older species R. pachyrhynchus is known from Oligocene and Miocene deposits in Pakistan's Bugti and Laki Hills and possibly the Khari Nadi Formation of Kutch.
Rhamphosuchus crassidens may have lived during the Late Pliocene and Early Middle Pleistocene based on associated fauna like Camelus sivalensis and Ursus sivalensis.
Fossils referred to Rhamphosuchus crassidens from Nepal are roughly Middle Pliocene in age and found in strata correlated to the Tatrot/Pinjor faunal zone of India and the Upper Siwaliks in Pakistan.
It is debated whether the bitemarks on rhino fossils belong to Rhamphosuchus, as other large crocodilians shared the same environment.
Jason J. Head suggests the hypodigm of Rhamphosuchus could be chimeric, with some specimens belonging to a different animal.
Courville and colleagues are hesitant to assign certain Nepalese remains to Rhamphosuchus crassidens, referring them instead to cf. Rhamphosuchus sp. due to tooth spacing.
